name: Alutiiq
packetScope: Kodiak-focused historical evidence: one renewed substantive web synthesis, three new substantive works read in selected passages, and one renewed short supporting lesson. No Site or canonical edits.

sources.title: Our Stories: Deep History
sources.annotation: The museum's substantial deep-history synthesis explains changing Kodiak technologies, fishing and household organization. Archaeological traditions describe ways of living rather than modern governments. Linked films, books and lessons do not automatically become additional inspected sources.
sources.contentReviewScope: Actual HTML Deep History body, lines 94–124, including Ocean Bay, Kachemak and Koniag sections; navigation and linked-media descriptions also checked.

sources.title: Cod Fishing in Russian America: The Archaeology of a 19th-Century Alutiiq Work Camp on Alaska’s Kodiak Island
sources.publisher: Arctic Anthropology / University of Wisconsin Press; author-uploaded reading copy on ResearchGate
sources.author: Amy V. Margaris, Mark A. Rusk, Patrick G. Saltonstall and Molly Odell
sources.annotation: Combines archaeological evidence and historical records to interpret a small seasonal company work camp. Its analysis distinguishes imposed labor from workers' continuing skills and choices. Conclusions are a site-specific interpretation, not proof of identical conditions in every Alutiiq community.
sources.contentReviewScope: Selected actual article text: introduction and colonial-labor passages, printed pages 102–105; Discussion and Conclusions passages, pages 121–123. Oberlin metadata verified; full-text host identifies upload by Amy Margaris on August 10, 2015.

sources.title: Teaching Traditions: Public Programming at the Alutiiq Museum
sources.publisher: Smithsonian Institution, National Museum of the American Indian, in Living Homes for Cultural Expression
sources.author: Amy F. Steffian; volume edited by Karen Coody Cooper and Nicolasa I. Sandoval
sources.annotation: A substantial museum practitioner's account of community archaeology, heritage organizing and choices about public education. It records disagreements and an Alutiiq-first mission rather than presenting revival as an outside discovery. Program examples and institutional circumstances are dated to this 2006 chapter.
sources.contentReviewScope: Selected actual chapter passages: opening pages 27–28; Programs Create the Museum, pages 32–33; A Philosophy for Programming, pages 34–35; and public-education examples, pages 36–37. Title/copyright pages checked. Not a full-volume review.

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Long coastal histories and archaeological interpretation
claimBlocks.text: The museum traces Kodiak's settlement back at least 7,800 years and describes Ocean Bay, Kachemak and Koniag traditions as changing ways of living. Its account connects sea-mammal hunting and cod fishing with later intensification of salmon harvesting, storage and exchange. Large shared houses accompanied later household cooperation. These archaeological labels organize evidence about technologies and communities; they should not be treated as three successive modern tribes or projected uniformly across the wider Sugpiaq homeland.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Deep History, Ocean Bay, Kachemak and Koniag sections

claimBlocks.text: The museum's short Awa’uq history places the 1784 Russian assault within a project to secure Native labor for the fur trade. It describes violence, hostage-taking and the subsequent imposition of work on women and men. Hunger and introduced diseases compounded the damage. This account offers an introduction to colonial conquest, while its numerical estimates and the details of later village consolidation require more focused historical reading than this brief lesson alone provides.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: One-page lesson, narrative from Shelikhov's arrival through colonial aftermath

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Archaeology of colonial labor and continuing knowledge
claimBlocks.text: Margaris and colleagues interpret a Kodiak house and associated food remains as evidence of a seasonal Russian-American Company work camp in the 1830s. Cod fishing and trapping helped provision the colonial enterprise. Yet repaired imported ceramics, reworked glass and other evidence indicate continuing Alutiiq technical knowledge and some pursuit of residents' own subsistence needs. Their study shows how coercive work arrangements could coexist with practical choices; imported objects alone do not demonstrate cultural replacement.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Printed pages 102–105 and Discussion and Conclusions, pages 121–123

claimBlocks.text: In a 2006 account, museum practitioner Amy Steffian connects Kodiak heritage organizing with community archaeology, youth participation and public sharing of research. Programs preceded the museum building. Later, leaders debated how collaboration with outside institutions could serve Alutiiq priorities. The resulting emphasis placed Alutiiq people first while inviting wider education. This history makes cultural renewal a matter of community decisions, institutions and sustained work, rather than suggesting that archaeologists discovered a people who had disappeared.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Programs Create the Museum, pages 32–33; A Philosophy for Programming, pages 34–35

claimBlocks.suggestedSection: Knowledge and unequal opportunity in the American era
claimBlocks.text: April Counceller's history describes Alutiiq bear guides whose knowledge supported Kodiak's twentieth-century hunting businesses. Guiding could fit around commercial fishing and food harvesting, linking paid work with family livelihoods. Yet the author explains that licensing paperwork and written examinations prevented some experienced guides from operating their own businesses or receiving professional recognition. This selected account illustrates how expertise could remain essential while the institutions governing employment distributed authority and earnings unequally.
claimBlocks.sourceLocator: Americans chapter excerpt, printed pages 120 and 122

researchGaps: The material is predominantly Kodiak-focused. Other Alutiiq/Sugpiaq regions need their own community and historical works rather than automatic extension of Kodiak conclusions.
Pullar1992 and the original Black conquest study remain worthwhile unread leads; no paraphrase of their catalog abstracts is presented as inspection of the works.
The 2024 book's full Russian-conquest chapter was not read. The counted book source is transparently limited to a substantive selected American-era excerpt.

Further original public family accounts could balance archaeological and institutional interpretations. No current population, casualty tally, restricted narrative or archaeological access directions are asserted.

summary.countingNote: Our Stories is one web synthesis; associated links are not multiplied. The 2024 book is one work across its selected pages. The short Refuge Rock orientation remains outside the substantive minimum.
